chk_01dc8bdf902c91205f7f5af6f3a8e1899cbe.preview:
Amazon Bedrock endpoints

Amazon Bedrock supports two endpoints for inference:

bedrock-mantle.{region}.api.aws — Supports the OpenAI-compatible Chat Completions and Responses APIs, and the Anthropic Messages API.

bedrock-runtime.{region}.amazonaws.com — Supports the Bedrock-native InvokeModel and Converse APIs, the OpenAI-compatible Chat Completions and Responses APIs, and the Anthropic Messages API.

For most new applications, start with bedrock-runtime. Use bedrock-mantle when you need capabilities that are available only on that endpoint, such as server-side tools, background inference, Projects, Workspaces, or a model that is available only on bedrock-mantle. You can use both endpoints in the same application. For a complete comparison, see Inference endpoints supported by Amazon Bed

chk_0ce9c6b6adf314bdadee7834c521a8e735fe.preview:
Regional availability and cross-Region inference

On-demand capacity is Regional and can vary across Regions. If your workload targets a single Region, it can encounter capacity errors during periods of high demand. With bedrock-runtime, use Global cross-Region inference when the model and your data-residency requirements support it. If you implement your own Regional failover, verify model availability in every target Region and apply bounded retries so that failover does not create a traffic surge.
chk_0ce9c6b6adf314bdadee7834c521a8e735fe.title: Scaling and throughput best practices

chk_1a16dc2708854d096f340a3d9aa523bac579.preview:
Why the two endpoints behave differently

Both endpoint surfaces use the same underlying inference engine, but their quota accounting and capacity options differ. bedrock-runtime uses per-model token quotas and, for some models, requests-per-minute (RPM) quotas. bedrock-mantle does not enforce RPM quotas and uses separate input-token and output-token quotas for models that have published quotas. Other models on bedrock-mantle might not have per-account quotas exposed in Service Quotas, but their throughput is still governed by internal service capacity.

Recommended ramp-up procedure

Estimate the target token rate and concurrency for each endpoint, model, and Region. For bedrock-mantle, track input and output tokens separately and include the requested max_tokens value in the input-token admission estimate.

Begin at a known stable baseline below the target. If you do not have a baseline, start with a small representative load instead of sending the full target volume.

Hold each level long enough to observe request success, 429/503/529 errors, latency percentiles, token consumption, concurrency, and queue depth.

Increase one controlled step at a time. Change only one major load dimension at a time so that you can identify the cause of a regression.

chk_32f22c0cf729bb9c4f93963ad6573fac809c.preview:
bedrock-mantle endpoint: throughput and quotas

The bedrock-mantle endpoint has the following quota behavior:

Models with published quotas have separate per-model, per-Region input-tokens-per-minute and output-tokens-per-minute quotas.

The endpoint does not enforce RPM quotas. Two workloads with the same RPM can consume very different amounts of capacity, so plan and rate-limit by tokens and concurrency instead of RPM alone.

When a request is admitted, the input-token check includes the input tokens plus the requested max_tokens value. After the response completes, the unused part of that reservation is replenished. Set max_tokens no higher than your application needs.

chk_49d9b05d1060c202b048461b6c8c2a572e5e.preview:
bedrock-runtime endpoint: throughput and quotas

The bedrock-runtime endpoint has the following quota behavior:

Per-model, per-Region token quotas count input and output tokens together. Output tokens consume quota according to a model-specific burndown rate.

Some models also have RPM quotas, while other models are governed only by token quotas. Check the quotas that apply to the exact model and inference profile that you use.

Per-minute and per-day token quotas are shared across the inference APIs that call the same model on this endpoint. Allocations for bedrock-runtime and bedrock-mantle are independent.

Custom inference profiles, batch inference, and Provisioned Throughput have separate quotas and are available only through bedrock-runtime.

Summary of recommendations

Scenario | Recommendation
Scenario: General workloads | Recommendation: Start with bedrock-runtime. Use bedrock-mantle for capabilities or models that require it. See Inference endpoints supported by Amazon Bedrock.
Scenario: Transient 429, 503, or 529 errors | Recommendation: Inspect the API error type. For retryable errors, honor Retry-After and retry with exponential backoff and jitter within a bounded retry budget.
Scenario: Sustained capacity errors | Recommendation: Stop ramping, return to the last stable level, bound concurrency and queues, defer lower-priority work, and use cross-Region inference where supported.

chk_9165039c84bd97eacccbbd5ad7009c0bccd3.preview:
Ramping up throughput

On-demand capacity can vary by model, Region, and time. Not all requests within a quota are guaranteed to succeed during periods of high demand, so ramp gradually when launching a workload, changing models or Regions, or making a large traffic increase. This is especially important for bedrock-mantle models that do not have a published per-account quota.
chk_9165039c84bd97eacccbbd5ad7009c0bccd3.title: Scaling and throughput best practices

chk_96f14818a828d3e06ff43ed3f690a7df6701.preview:
Additional best practices

Use feature flags to gradually transition traffic between models rather than switching all traffic at once.

Spread large workloads across multiple minutes and consider time-of-day patterns to avoid peak usage periods.

Test with representative distributions of input size, output size, latency, and concurrency. Avoid sending a sudden burst of test requests.

Use token-aware client-side rate limiting, bounded concurrency, and bounded queues. An RPM-only limiter does not protect against changes in request size.

For asynchronous, high-volume offline jobs, use batch inference on bedrock-runtime.

For supported models and non-time-sensitive requests that can tolerate variable latency, consider the Flex service tier.
chk_96f14818a828d3e06ff43ed3f690a7df6701.title: Scaling and throughput best practices

chk_cb9908486f900677d038446848c76ebdf423.preview:
Sustained capacity errors

If you receive persistent 503 or 529 errors, retries alone can amplify load. The service might be experiencing a temporary capacity constraint, or the workload might exceed the capacity currently available for the model and Region. Take the following steps:

Stop the ramp and return to the last stable request rate and concurrency level.

Use bounded client-side concurrency, rate limiting, and request queues.

Defer or shed lower-priority requests until capacity recovers.

For bedrock-runtime, use cross-Region inference when the model supports it. For predictable, sustained workloads, evaluate Provisioned Throughput.

If the problem continues, check the AWS Health Dashboard and contact AWS Support with request IDs and UTC timestamps.
chk_cb9908486f900677d038446848c76ebdf423.title: Scaling and throughput best practices

chk_e6c92ac8caefd2bddd53345758c6ba11865f.preview:
Handling demand shocks

Some applications experience sudden large shocks in demand. This happens for a variety of reasons: a news event, big sale, media event, or some other event that goes viral and causes traffic to quickly and significantly increase in a very short span of time. If unplanned, this can cause demand to quickly outstrip available resources.

The best way to handle demand shocks is to anticipate them and plan accordingly. Because autoscaling can take time, we recommend that you scale out your application before the demand shock begins. For the best results, we recommend having a business plan that involves tight collaboration between teams that use a shared calender. The team that's planning the event should work closely with the team in charge of the application in advance
chk_e6c92ac8caefd2bddd53345758c6ba11865f.title: Amazon ECS capacity and availability

chk_fe3f01e7746c9e7dbecd3dffe3e451100622.preview:
Example Retry configuration for bedrock-mantle (Anthropic SDK)

```
import anthropic

client = anthropic.Anthropic(
    api_key=api_key,
    base_url=f"https://bedrock-mantle.{region}.api.aws/anthropic",
    max_retries=5,
)
```

Configure connection and read timeouts separately from retries, based on the model and operation's documented maximum inference duration. A timeout that is shorter than a valid long-running inference request can cause avoidable retries and duplicate work.
chk_fe3f01e7746c9e7dbecd3dffe3e451100622.title: Scaling and throughput best practices

chk_ff329b1790a8b398c46d12ce9f3c6a440ac0.preview:
Understanding HTTP error responses

HTTP 429

A 429 response means that the request was not admitted. Inspect the API-specific error type rather than relying on the HTTP status alone. A ThrottlingException or rate-limit error generally means that the request exceeded an account quota or a service rate limit. Some runtime operations also use HTTP 429 for ModelNotReadyException. On bedrock-mantle, check input and output TPM usage and the request's max_tokens value; the endpoint does not have an RPM quota. On bedrock-runtime, check combined token quotas and RPM, if the model has an RPM quota.
